title: Chapter 16 — Why The National Vanity Of The Americans Is More Restless And Captious Than That Of The English
paragraphs: And Captious Than That of the English

All free nations are vainglorious, but not all show their national pride in the same way. In their dealings with foreigners, the Americans seem unable to bear the smallest criticism and can never get enough praise. The slightest compliment pleases them; the most extravagant rarely satisfies them. They press you incessantly to wring praise out of you, and if you resist their pleading they begin to praise themselves. It seems as if, doubting their own merit, they want it displayed before their eyes at every moment. Their vanity is not only greedy but restless and jealous; it grants nothing while demanding everything, and is ready to beg and to quarrel at the same time. If I tell an American that the country he lives in is a fine one, “Ay,” he replies, “there is not its fellow in the world.” If I applaud the freedom its inhabitants enjoy, he answers, “Freedom is a fine thing, but few nations are worthy to enjoy it.” If I remark on the purity of morals that distinguishes the United States, “I can imagine,” says he, “that a stranger, who has been struck by the corruption of all other nations, is astonished at the difference.” At last I leave him to admire himself; but he comes back to the attack and does not let up until he has made me repeat everything I had just said. It is impossible to imagine a more tiresome or more talkative patriotism; it wearies even those who are inclined to respect it. *a

The English are not like this. An Englishman calmly enjoys the advantages, real or imagined, that he believes his country has. If he grants nothing to other nations, neither does he ask anything for his own. The criticism of foreigners does not affect him, and their praise hardly flatters him. His attitude toward the rest of the world is one of disdainful, uninformed reserve; his pride needs no feeding, for it nourishes itself. It is remarkable that two nations that sprang so recently from the same stock should be so opposite in their way of feeling and talking.

In aristocratic countries the great hold immense privileges, on which their pride rests, without seeking to rely on the lesser advantages that come to them. Because these privileges reached them by inheritance, they regard them in some sense as part of themselves, or at least as a natural right belonging to their own persons. They therefore have a calm sense of their superiority. They do not dream of boasting about privileges that everyone sees and no one disputes, and these things are not new enough to them to be worth talking about. They stand unmoved in their solitary greatness, confident that all the world sees them without any effort on their part to show themselves off, and that no one will try to dislodge them. When an aristocracy conducts the public affairs, its national pride naturally takes this reserved, indifferent, and haughty form, which all the other classes of the nation imitate.

When, on the contrary, social conditions differ only a little, the slightest privileges matter. Since every man sees around him a million people enjoying exactly the same or similar advantages, his pride becomes greedy and jealous; he clings to mere trifles and defends them stubbornly. In democracies, because the conditions of life fluctuate so much, men have almost always acquired their advantages recently. The result is that they take extreme pleasure in displaying them, to show others and to persuade themselves that they truly enjoy them. Since these same advantages may be lost at any moment, their owners are constantly on the alert and make a point of showing that they still hold them. Men living in democracies love their country just as they love themselves, and they carry over the habits of their private vanity into their vanity as a nation. The restless, insatiable vanity of a democratic people comes so entirely from the equality and precariousness of social conditions that the members of the haughtiest nobility show exactly the same passion in those lesser parts of their existence where anything is fluctuating or contested. An aristocratic class always differs greatly from the other classes of the nation in the extent and permanence of its privileges; but it often happens that the only differences among its own members lie in small, passing advantages that may be lost or gained any day. Members of a powerful aristocracy, gathered in a capital or at a court, have been known to fight bitterly over those frivolous privileges that depend on the whim of fashion or the will of their master. These persons then showed one another exactly the same childish jealousies that move the men of democracies: the same eagerness to snatch the smallest advantages their equals disputed, and the same wish to parade the ones they already held. If national pride ever entered the minds of courtiers, I have no doubt that they would show it in the same way as the members of a democratic community.
